sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays.pattern: Contribution technique: index i is in (i + 1)(n − i) subarrays, about half of them odd-length

approaches.name: Sum every odd-length subarray
approaches.idea: Try every start and every odd length, and add up the elements of each subarray with an inner loop.
steps: For every start `l` and every end `r ≥ l` with `r − l` even (odd length):
add `arr[l] + … + arr[r]` to the total with a third loop.
approaches.why: About n²/4 subarrays, each summed in O(n). Fine for n = 100, but the work per subarray is repeated over and over.

approaches.name: Prefix sums
approaches.idea: Precompute prefix sums so each subarray sum is p[r + 1] − p[l] in O(1).
steps: Build `p` with `p[i + 1] = p[i] + arr[i]`.
For every start `l` and odd-length end `r`, add `p[r + 1] − p[l]`.
approaches.why: Each subarray is now O(1), but there are still O(n²) of them.

approaches.name: Contribution of each element
approaches.idea: arr[i] is in (i + 1)(n − i) subarrays (starts × ends); ⌈that / 2⌉ of them have odd length. Add arr[i] times that count.
steps: For each `i`, `all = (i + 1) × (n − i)` subarrays contain it.
Odd length means start and end have the same parity, which is `(all + 1) / 2` of them.
Add `arr[i] × (all + 1) / 2`.
approaches.why: One pass and a little arithmetic per element: the sum is reorganised by element instead of by subarray.

number-of-zero-filled-subarrays.pattern: Contribution technique: credit each all-zero subarray to its right end

approaches.name: Extend from every start
approaches.idea: From every start, extend to the right while the elements are zero; each step is one more all-zero subarray.
steps: For each start `l`: walk `r = l, l + 1, …` while `nums[r] == 0`.
Count one subarray per step.
approaches.why: An array of 10⁵ zeros makes every start walk to the end: about 5 × 10⁹ steps.

approaches.name: Length of the current zero run
approaches.idea: If the run of zeros ending at i has length run, exactly run all-zero subarrays end at i. Add run at every index.
steps: Keep `run`: `run + 1` on a zero, `0` otherwise.
Add `run` to the total at every index (64-bit).
approaches.why: Every all-zero subarray is counted once, at its right end, so one pass suffices.

vowels-of-all-substrings.pattern: Contribution technique: a vowel at i is in (i + 1)(n − i) substrings

approaches.name: Every substring with a running count
approaches.idea: Fix the start, extend the end one character at a time while counting vowels, and add the running count for each substring.
steps: For each start `l`, set `vowels = 0`.
For each end `r ≥ l`: add 1 if `word[r]` is a vowel, then add `vowels` to the total.
approaches.why: There are about n²/2 substrings: 5 × 10⁹ for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Contribution of each vowel
approaches.idea: A substring containing index i starts in 0 … i and ends in i … n − 1, so a vowel at i is counted (i + 1) × (n − i) times.
steps: For each index `i` holding a vowel, add `(i + 1) × (n − i)`.
Use 64-bit arithmetic: the product reaches 2.5 × 10⁹.
approaches.why: Each character is looked at once, and its contribution is a product of two counts.

total-hamming-distance.pattern: Contribution technique per bit: bit b adds ones × zeros

approaches.name: Every pair
approaches.idea: For every pair, count the set bits of a ^ b.
steps: For every pair `i < j`: add `bitCount(nums[i] ^ nums[j])`.
Return the total.
approaches.why: n = 10⁴ gives 5 × 10⁷ pairs: borderline, and the per-bit view is much faster.

approaches.name: Count ones per bit
approaches.idea: Bits are independent. At bit b, with ones numbers having a 1, exactly ones × (n − ones) pairs differ there.
steps: For each bit `b` from 0 to 31: count `ones`.
Add `ones × (n − ones)`.
approaches.why: Each pair is never looked at directly: it is counted once per bit where it differs, through the column counts.

bitwise-xor-of-all-pairings.pattern: Contribution technique with XOR parity: each value appears (other length) times

approaches.name: XOR every pair
approaches.idea: Loop over every (i, j) and XOR nums1[i] ^ nums2[j] into the answer.
steps: For every `a` in `nums1` and `b` in `nums2`: `x ^= a ^ b`.
Return `x`.
approaches.why: Up to 10¹⁰ pairs for two arrays of 10⁵.

approaches.name: Only odd counts survive
approaches.idea: Each nums1 value is XOR-ed nums2.length times and each nums2 value nums1.length times; an even count cancels to 0.
steps: If `nums2.length` is odd, XOR every element of `nums1` into the answer.
If `nums1.length` is odd, XOR every element of `nums2` into the answer.
approaches.why: Contribution by value: only whether a value appears an odd number of times matters for XOR.

sum-of-absolute-differences-in-a-sorted-.pattern: Contribution technique with prefix sums: sorted, so |x − y| splits into a left and a right part

approaches.name: Sum each row directly
approaches.idea: For every i, loop over every j and add |nums[i] − nums[j]|.
steps: For each `i`: `res[i] = Σ |nums[i] − nums[j]|` over all `j`.
Return `res`.
approaches.why: 10¹⁰ operations for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Prefix sums on both sides
approaches.idea: Everything before i is ≤ nums[i] and everything after is ≥ it, so res[i] = (nums[i]·i − sum before) + (sum after − nums[i]·(n − 1 − i)).
steps: Build prefix sums `p` with `p[i + 1] = p[i] + nums[i]`.
Left part: `nums[i] × i − p[i]`.
Right part: `(p[n] − p[i + 1]) − nums[i] × (n − 1 − i)`; add both.
approaches.why: The sort removes the absolute value, and prefix sums give each side's total in O(1).

sum-of-distances.pattern: Contribution technique with prefix sums, per group of equal values

approaches.name: Compare every pair of indices
approaches.idea: For every i, scan every j with the same value and add |i − j|.
steps: For each `i`, loop over all `j`.
If `nums[j] == nums[i]`, add `|i − j|` to `res[i]`.
approaches.why: 10¹⁰ comparisons for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Group indices, then prefix sums
approaches.idea: Collect the (sorted) indices of each value. For the k-th index j in a group: (j·k − sum before) + (sum after − j·(size − 1 − k)).
steps: Group indices by value with a hash map (left to right, so each list is sorted).
For each group, compute its total and walk it with a running sum of the indices before.
Set `res[j] = (j·k − left) + (right − j·(size − 1 − k))`.
approaches.why: Every index is handled once in its group, with O(1) work from the running sums.

subarray-product-less-than-k.pattern: Sliding window + contribution: right end r adds r − l + 1

approaches.name: Extend from every start
approaches.idea: From each start, multiply in elements to the right until the product reaches k (positive values only grow it).
steps: For each start `l`, set `prod = 1`.
Extend `r` while `prod × nums[r] < k`, counting each step; stop as soon as it reaches `k`.
approaches.why: With many 1s every start walks almost to the end: about 4.5 × 10⁸ steps for 3 × 10⁴ ones.

approaches.name: Sliding window, count at the right end
approaches.idea: Keep the window [l, r] with product < k. Every subarray ending at r and starting in [l, r] is valid: r − l + 1 of them.
steps: If `k ≤ 1`, return 0.
For each `r`: multiply in `nums[r]`, then divide out `nums[l++]` while the product is `≥ k`.
Add `r − l + 1`.
approaches.why: Each index enters and leaves the window once, and each valid subarray is credited exactly once, to its right end.

count-subarrays-where-max-element-appear.pattern: Sliding window + contribution: for "at least", right end r adds l

approaches.name: Count copies from every start
approaches.idea: From each start, extend to the right counting copies of the maximum; once there are k, every longer subarray also qualifies.
steps: Find the maximum `m`.
For each start `l`, extend `r` counting copies of `m`; when the count reaches `k`, add `n − r` and stop.
approaches.why: When copies of the maximum are rare, each start walks far: up to 5 × 10⁹ steps.

approaches.name: Sliding window, count valid starts
approaches.idea: For each r, shrink from the left while the window still holds k copies. Then every start before l keeps at least k copies, so r contributes l.
steps: Find the maximum `m`; keep `seen` = copies of `m` in `[l, r]`.
For each `r`: count `nums[r]`; while `seen ≥ k`, drop `nums[l++]`.
Add `l`: starts `0 … l − 1` all work for this `r`.
approaches.why: Both pointers only move forward, and each valid subarray is credited once, to its right end.

sum-of-subarray-ranges.pattern: Contribution technique: sum of maximums − sum of minimums, each with monotonic stacks

approaches.name: Every subarray, scanned
approaches.idea: For every subarray, scan it for its minimum and maximum.
steps: For every `l ≤ r`: scan `nums[l..r]` for min and max.
Add `max − min`.
approaches.why: About n³/6 operations: 1.7 × 10⁸ for n = 1000.

approaches.name: Running min and max
approaches.idea: Fix the start and extend the end, updating the running minimum and maximum in O(1).
steps: For each `l`, start `mn = mx = nums[l]`.
For each `r ≥ l`, update `mn` and `mx` with `nums[r]` and add `mx − mn`.
approaches.why: Fast enough for n = 1000 (5 × 10⁵ subarrays), and what most people write first; the follow-up asks for O(n).

approaches.name: Contribution with monotonic stacks
approaches.idea: Range sum = Σ maximums − Σ minimums. a[i] is the minimum of (i − prev smaller) × (next smaller-or-equal − i) subarrays; likewise for maximums.
steps: With a monotonic stack, find for each `i` the previous strictly smaller index and the next smaller-or-equal index (the tie rule stops double counting).
Sum `a[i] × (i − prev) × (next − i)` for minimums; repeat with the comparisons flipped for maximums.
Return maximums − minimums.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed and popped once per pass, and every subarray is credited to exactly one minimum and one maximum.

minimum-fuel-cost-to-report-to-the-capit.pattern: Contribution of each tree edge: the road above v costs ⌈size(v) / seats⌉

approaches.name: Walk every representative up
approaches.idea: For every city, walk its path to the capital and add one person to each road it uses; then each road costs ⌈people / seats⌉.
steps: Root the tree at 0 (BFS) to get each city's parent.
For every city `v`, walk `v → parent → … → 0`, adding 1 to `people` on each road (stored at the lower city).
Add `⌈people[v] / seats⌉` for every non-capital city.
approaches.why: On a path of 10⁵ cities the walks add up to about 5 × 10⁹ steps.

approaches.name: Subtree sizes in one traversal
approaches.idea: The people crossing the road above v are exactly v's subtree, so that road costs ⌈size(v) / seats⌉. Compute every subtree size bottom-up.
steps: BFS from the capital to get a parent array and an order (parents before children).
Walk the order backwards: `size[v] += 1`, add `⌈size[v] / seats⌉`, then push `size[v]` into its parent.
approaches.why: Each road's cost depends only on its subtree size, and one bottom-up pass gives all of them; iterative so a 10⁵-city path can't overflow the stack.

sum-of-subsequence-widths.pattern: Contribution after sorting: a[i] is the max of 2^i and the min of 2^(n−1−i) subsequences

approaches.name: Every subsequence
approaches.idea: Enumerate all 2ⁿ − 1 non-empty subsets with a bitmask and add max − min for each.
steps: For every mask from 1 to `2ⁿ − 1`, scan the chosen elements for min and max.
Add `max − min` modulo 10⁹ + 7.
approaches.why: Exponential: hopeless beyond n ≈ 20, while n goes up to 10⁵.

approaches.name: Sort, then powers of two
approaches.idea: Width = max − min, and only the chosen values matter, so sort. Then nums[i] adds nums[i] × (2^i − 2^(n−1−i)).
steps: Sort `nums` and precompute `pow2[k] = 2^k mod 10⁹ + 7`.
Add `nums[i] × (pow2[i] − pow2[n − 1 − i])` for every `i`, modulo 10⁹ + 7.
The running total may be negative: add the modulus before the final `%`.
approaches.why: Counting subsets by who their max and min are replaces 2ⁿ subsets with n contributions.

total-appeal-of-a-string.pattern: Contribution technique: credit the first copy of each letter, (i − last) × (n − i)

approaches.name: Every substring with a seen set
approaches.idea: Fix the start, extend the end, and track the distinct letters seen so far; add that count for every substring.
steps: For each start `l`, clear a 26-entry `seen` array and set `distinct = 0`.
For each end `r ≥ l`: mark `s[r]` (counting it if new) and add `distinct`.
approaches.why: About 5 × 10⁹ substrings for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Last-seen positions
approaches.idea: s[i] is the first copy of its letter in a substring exactly when the substring starts after the letter's previous occurrence: (i − last) starts × (n − i) ends.
steps: Keep `last[26]`, initialised to −1.
For each `i`: add `(i − last[c]) × (n − i)`, then set `last[c] = i`.
approaches.why: Every substring's appeal is split among its letters' first copies, and each copy's share is a product of two counts.

count-unique-characters-of-all-substring.pattern: Contribution technique: s[i] counts between its previous and next copies, (i − prev) × (next − i)

approaches.name: Every substring with letter counts
approaches.idea: Fix the start and extend the end, keeping letter counts and the number of letters that appear exactly once.
steps: For each start `l`, clear the counts and set `unique = 0`.
For each end `r`: update `count[s[r]]` (1 → unique + 1, 2 → unique − 1) and add `unique`.
approaches.why: About 5 × 10⁹ substrings for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Previous and next occurrence
approaches.idea: s[i] is the only copy of its letter in substrings that start after the previous copy and end before the next one: (i − prev[i]) × (next[i] − i).
steps: Left to right, record `prev[i]` (−1 if none); right to left, `next[i]` (n if none).
Add `(i − prev[i]) × (next[i] − i)` for every `i`.
approaches.why: Each letter copy's contribution is a product of two distances, so no substring is ever listed.

count-subarrays-with-score-less-than-k.pattern: Sliding window + contribution: right end r adds r − l + 1

approaches.name: Extend from every start
approaches.idea: From each start, extend to the right with a running sum; stop once sum × length reaches k (it only grows).
steps: For each start `l`, keep a running `sum`.
Extend `r` while `sum × (r − l + 1) < k`, counting each step.
approaches.why: With small values and a huge k, every start walks to the end: about 5 × 10⁹ steps.

approaches.name: Sliding window, count at the right end
approaches.idea: Keep the longest window ending at r with score < k; every subarray ending at r inside it is valid: r − l + 1 of them.
steps: Add `nums[r]` to `sum`.
While `sum × (r − l + 1) ≥ k`, subtract `nums[l++]`.
Add `r − l + 1` (64-bit).
approaches.why: Positive values make validity monotone, so each pointer only moves forward and each subarray is counted once.

sum-of-total-strength-of-wizards.pattern: Contribution with a monotonic stack + prefix sums of prefix sums

approaches.name: Every group with a running min and sum
approaches.idea: Fix the start and extend the end, keeping the running minimum and sum; add min × sum for each group.
steps: For each start `l`, set `mn = ∞` and `sum = 0`.
For each end `r`: update `mn` and `sum`, add `mn × sum` modulo 10⁹ + 7.
approaches.why: About 5 × 10⁹ groups for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Stack spans + prefix of prefix sums
approaches.idea: Credit each group to its weakest wizard (strict on the left, non-strict on the right). For i, the groups are starts prev+1 … i and ends i … next−1; their sums total (i − prev)·ΣP[i+1..next] − (next − i)·ΣP[prev+1..i].
steps: Monotonic stack: previous strictly smaller index `prev[i]`, next smaller-or-equal index `next[i]`.
Prefix sums `P` and prefix sums of those, `PP`, all modulo 10⁹ + 7.
For each `i`, combine the two `PP` ranges as above and add `strength[i] ×` the result.
approaches.why: The stack gives each wizard's span in O(n) total, and PP turns "sum of all group sums in the span" into O(1).

sum-of-distances-in-tree.pattern: Edge contribution for the root, then rerooting

approaches.name: BFS from every node
approaches.idea: Run a BFS from each node and add up the distances it finds.
steps: Build the adjacency list.
For every node `s`, BFS and set `ans[s]` = sum of distances.
approaches.why: 9 × 10⁸ steps for n = 3 × 10⁴.

approaches.name: Subtree sizes, then rerooting
approaches.idea: ans[0] = Σ size[v] over non-root v (each node below an edge uses it once to reach 0). Moving the root to a child c: ans[c] = ans[parent] − size[c] + (n − size[c]).
steps: BFS from 0 for parents and an order; walk it backwards to get subtree sizes and `ans[0]`.
Walk the order forwards: `ans[v] = ans[parent[v]] − size[v] + (n − size[v])`.
approaches.why: Edge contribution gives one answer in O(n), and each reroot step changes it in O(1); both passes are iterative, so deep trees are safe.
